turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break it down simply. When you’re choosing a rose, you’re mainly deciding between a few big options:

Type/shape of rose
Shrub/bush roses: Round, bushy plants. Great for most gardens and beginners. Good for beds, borders, or by a walkway.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need support (fence, trellis, arch, pergola). Good if you want height or a “wall” of blooms.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low, spreading plants that cover an area. Nice for slopes, edges, or filling space.
Size
Every product page lists height and width in feet.
Think about how much room you have so it doesn’t outgrow the spot.
Bloom habit
Repeat or continuous bloomers: Flower over and over through the season. These are perfect for beginners because you see lots of blooms.
Once-blooming: A big flush of flowers once a year. Beautiful, but not as “constant” for new growers.
Sun and climate
Full sun = at least 6 hours of direct sun per day. Most roses want this.
Use your hardiness zone at the top of our website so you only see roses that handle your winters.

turns.replyText:
Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

Great question, and you’re smart to think about this before you buy anything.

Here’s a simple “beginner starter kit” list.

Absolute must-haves
Sunny spot outdoors: At least 6 hours of direct sun per day.
Well-draining soil: Not soggy after rain; you can improve it with amendments (see below).
Basic tools: A shovel for digging, hand pruners for trimming, and a watering can or hose.
Mulch: A 2–3" layer of bark or other organic mulch helps keep soil moisture even and protects roots.
Soil amendments (optional but very helpful) These improve soil structure and long-term health, but you can start without all of them if budget is tight.
Bone meal: Helps strong root development when planting.
Cow manure: Adds long-lasting nutrients to the soil.
Mint compost: Lightens and aerates the soil and can be used on top as protection for roots.
Worm castings: Gentle, slow-release nutrients and better soil aeration.
Living soil: A rich planting medium you can mix into your native soil.

All of these are optional, but using one or two (like compost plus bone meal) gives your rose a very nice head start. If you order them from us, you can select your estimated delivery date at checkout so they arrive when you’re ready to plant.

Fertilizer (this one really is needed) Fertilizing is important for healthy growth and blooms.
In the first year, a liquid fertilizer is especially helpful because it is easier for young roots to use.
We offer options like OmniMeal, Founders Fish Fertilizer, and Boost & Bloom, but you can use any good rose fertilizer you prefer.
Start once the plant is actively growing and follow the directions on the label.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

You’re so close to having your first rose, which is exciting. Here’s how to use it “right” from day one, in simple steps.

I’ll describe the basics for both ground and container planting. If you tell me your zip code and whether you’ll use a pot or plant in the ground, I can fine-tune this for you.

Timing
Plant outdoors only.
Put it in the ground after your last spring frost or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
If it arrives and it is not a safe planting time, move it from the shipping pot into a larger container (about 10 inches across) and keep it outdoors in a protected spot.
Unpacking your rose
Your rose will arrive in a 1‑gallon container with soil and will likely have no leaves or buds at first. That is normal.
Take it out of the box and water it so the soil is evenly moist (not soggy).
Let it sit in bright outdoor light for a day or so before planting if you can, just to recover from shipping.
Choosing the spot
Pick a place with at least 6 hours of direct sun each day (full sun).
Make sure the area drains well. Water should not sit around the plant.
Planting in the ground (first time)
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep.
Mix the top soil from the hole with some organic material if you have it (compost, well-rotted manure, or similar).
Do not use potting soil that already has granular or time‑release fertilizer mixed in for the planting hole; that can burn young roots.
Gently remove the rose from its container and set it in the hole so the soil level in the pot matches the soil level of the ground.
Backfill with your soil mix and press gently to remove big air pockets.
Water deeply so everything settles.
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch around, but keep it a couple inches away from the base of the plant.
Planting in a container (first time)
Choose a large pot with drainage:
For a bush rose: 10–15 gallons.
For a climber: roughly 2 ft x 2 ft, around 20–25 gallons.
Fill with a good organic potting soil that does not include granular or time‑release fertilizer.
Place the rose so the existing soil surface from the nursery pot is level with the new soil surface.
Water until water drains out the bottom and the soil is evenly moist.
Watering in the first weeks
For the first few weeks, water 2–3 times per week, depending on your weather.
Always water at the base of the plant, not over the leaves.
Aim for soil that is moist but not constantly soggy.
Fertilizer, the very first time
Wait until you see new growth (little red or green shoots and leaves) before you start fertilizing.
For the first year, use a liquid fertilizer (gentler for young roots). A good example from us is Founders Fish Fertilizer.
Feed about every 2–3 weeks during the growing season, and stop 6–8 weeks before your first fall frost.
